title: Strategy pattern: interchangeable algorithms with a TypeScript example — cv.cm
description: The Strategy pattern puts each algorithm in its own object so you can swap them at runtime. See classes vs functions in TypeScript, and when to use it.
answer: Strategy is a behavioral design pattern that defines a family of algorithms, puts each one in a separate object with a common interface, and makes them interchangeable. The code that uses an algorithm, called the context, holds a reference to a strategy and calls it without knowing which one it is. In TypeScript a strategy is often just a function, as in the comparator passed to `array.sort()`.

sections.h: Intent and the problem it solves
body: Intent: define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it. It is one of the behavioral patterns in the Gang of Four (GoF) book, where it is also called Policy.

Suppose a checkout calculates shipping cost. Standard shipping is a flat fee, express costs more per kilogram, and pickup in a store is free. A first version puts all three formulas in one method with an `if`/`else` chain on the shipping type. Each new option, such as a partner courier, means editing that method again, and testing one formula means going through all the others.

With Strategy, each formula becomes its own object or function with the same signature. The checkout receives the chosen strategy and calls it. Adding a courier means adding one new strategy; the checkout does not change.

sections.h: When to use it and when not to

ul: Use it when there are several ways to do the same task and the choice depends on configuration, user input or the data.
Use it to remove large conditional blocks that select between algorithms.
Use it to test each algorithm in isolation and to let other code add new algorithms without editing the context.
Do not use it when there is only one algorithm and no real need to change it. An extra interface adds indirection for nothing.
Do not create classes when a function parameter is enough. In TypeScript, passing a function is the lightweight form of Strategy.
`Array.prototype.sort(compareFn)` takes the comparison strategy as a function, so the same sort can order numbers, dates or names.
Java's `Comparator` interface is a strategy for `Collections.sort` and `List.sort`.
Passport.js, the authentication middleware for Node.js, calls each login method (local password, OAuth providers) a strategy and lets applications plug them in.
Compression and hashing libraries let callers choose an algorithm through a common interface.

head: Pattern
How it differs from Strategy
rows: Same structure, but states switch themselves as the object changes; a strategy is usually chosen by the client and stays until replaced.
Template Method varies parts of an algorithm through inheritance and fixes the overall steps; Strategy replaces the whole algorithm through composition.
A command is a request to run later; a strategy is a way of performing a task that the context calls when needed.
A decorator changes an object's behavior by wrapping it from the outside; a strategy changes behavior from the inside by replacing one part.

faq.q: What is the difference between Strategy and State?
faq.a: The structures are almost identical. A strategy is picked by the client to choose how a task is done, while state objects change the context's current state themselves as a result of its actions.

faq.q: Is passing a callback the Strategy pattern?
faq.a: Yes, in languages with first-class functions a callback that implements a variable part of an algorithm, such as a comparator, is the Strategy pattern in its simplest form.

faq.q: What is the difference between Strategy and Template Method?
faq.a: Template Method uses inheritance: a base class fixes the steps and subclasses fill in some of them. Strategy uses composition: the context holds an object or function that it can replace at runtime.

faq.q: Does Strategy follow the open/closed principle?
faq.a: Yes. You can add new strategies without changing the context, so the context is open for extension but closed for modification.
